scenes.said: Ghana just launched something called Marrify. It's like
a public platform where you can search and verify marriages, divorces and licensed marriage officials.
It launched last month with some Ministry of Gender,
and I was just reading about it the other day on TechCabal. And the way that it works is that it
pulls data from different government sources, the Registrar-General's Department, the courts, local assembly, all of that. It covers
all kinds of marriages and all kinds of divorces. It goes all the way back, like records from all the way back. And you can also
check whether a church or a pastor and a marriage venue is actually licensed to conduct a marriage.
And I really love this when I saw this, because as an African, I'm thinking, wow, we're having
centralised data, finally, finally!
Now before I talk about drawbacks, because I read TechCabal's article about this, and there were some drawbacks it cited.
I've been living in Estonia for about a year now, and people always say, like, this place is the digital hub of Europe or something like that.

And I'm not going to lie, it's so real. Everything here, everything you want to do here is online. I'm not exaggerating. Everything. Your health records, everything links so well. There is nothing you want to do that you can't do online here. You can get married online, you can divorce online. There's a link for everything you want to do in Estonia.
The data ecosystem that the governments use, that they run here, the way it syncs, I genuinely admire it.
And as someone coming from Nigeria, it blew my mind when I got it, where everything just syncs. And when I see something in this direction,
my first instinct is like, yes, please, more of this, because it solves so many problems.
There's one reliable record instead of like just pieces of paper everywhere, instead of NIN and this and that. And I think the main thing that even made me record this video is
the drawback that TechCabal raised, which is that marriage and divorce records are sensitive private data.
I don't know, like a divorce record is a personal thing about someone's life.
And now that record is searchable by anyone that has your name.

And I'm saying this as someone that likes open data. In Estonia, you can search online and find businesses. You can check how much a business, like, you don't know anything about, You can look up how much they made in a
year. And that's fine, I think, because if business is a public entity, that takes public money, holds public accountability.
But maybe in the case of a divorce, it's a little bit different.

So that really got me thinking about the drawbacks, of course. I don't really know, because I love the idea of open data, but I also really don't know how to balance it well with personal data and privacy issues.

And there's also the consent part of the conversation, like the difference between a divorce record sitting in a courthouse somewhere in 2003, and somebody just being able to check it on their phone in three seconds, right?
And I was also then thinking about data minimisation. So the idea of data minimisation is that you expose the minimum amount of data required to answer the question being asked.
So if I ask the question, is this person currently free to marry? That's a yes or no answer.
Answering that question does not require showing when they got married, who they married, when they divorced, which court granted it, right?
I was also thinking about how data minimisation can come to play here as well. Could we minimise data to the point where we are not exposing much more than it's been asked for?

Like in the case of Marrify in Ghana, for example, the question is, is this person married? So the answer is simple, this person currently has an active marriage on record. Nothing else, no name of spouse, no dates, no history.

But of course, another person could request another thing. And then I was thinking about like access level. Maybe perhaps an individual could access a level of this data and maybe there are certain organizations or institutions that can access more. I was just thinking about all of it.
And again, I always say this, that technology is not neutral. It works, it takes the form of the system or the place that you're using it in.

For example, the way a piece of technology works in Estonia will be completely different from the way it's working in a country in Africa, in Nigeria, in Ghana. In Estonia, a divorce record could just be administrative, nobody cares. But in an African context, to a large extent, divorce, especially for women, is pretty stigmatised.
So it's very tricky when I think about it, when I think about the drawbacks first, that this is something that I myself think I need to explore further, the human side of this thing.
It's not just a privacy engineering conversation, it's also a cultural design thing. But I've just been putting it side by side. I really love the idea,
but another thing I find genuinely smart in Estonia is the idea that your data being in the system is also paired with you being able to see what's happening to it.
That transparency runs both ways.
And I also think that if we are creating open data in Africa, we also need to ask the question of reciprocity. Where is the reciprocity for the average individual?
If someone looks up my marriage record, do I get to see that someone looked it up?
I really want African countries building this kind of infrastructure, because I genuinely think it also solves a problem. Technology helps when it comes to things like this.
But I also think that if we want to build this kind of infrastructure, as people, we still need to probe it a little bit and question it. And that's what I've just been doing in my head.
I really like the idea I read about. It's super, super cool. I really love it. But again, just thinking about the drawbacks and everything. this is just what's been running in my head. Yeah.
